issue.title: When a big chain fails, who looks after its workers and towns?
issue.question: When a big high street chain is failing, what should the government do for its workers and the towns it leaves behind?
issue.summary: Poundland, a chain of about 600 stores and 12,000 staff, is in sale talks, with a preferred bid due by Wednesday and a pause on creditors' demands due to end on Thursday. If a whole-company bid fails, the stores, staff and stock could be auctioned to rivals. Its owner Gordon Brothers released about £20m last week, and ITV News reported that £60m of sales cash is still out of reach. The Business Secretary is due to meet the owner next week.

bench.title: Workers paid first and fast, whoever buys or auctions the stores
bench.answer: The Business Secretary, who says intervention options are under review (s2), makes any sale or store auction (s1) conditional on workers being paid first, with no public money for owners. The Insolvency Service already aims to pay eligible employee claims within 6 weeks (s3); the Secretary makes that a hard limit. Contractors, who now queue as creditors (s4), get the same route through a rule change. Success: every eligible claim, contractors included, is paid within 6 weeks, and the department publishes the count of claims paid and days taken.

bench.title: Give staff and towns first call on stores before any auction
bench.answer: If a whole-company bid fails, Poundland's stores, staff and stock could be auctioned to rivals [s1]. Instead, the Business Secretary, who says his options are under review [s2], would give staff groups and local councils a short first right to take over any store due to close, with the Insolvency Service paying owed wages and notice directly [s3]. No public money goes to the owner or bosses; that limit had 51 backers among simulated citizens. Contractors, who must otherwise queue as creditors [s4], would be paid in the same round. It worked if workers were paid within 6 weeks [s3], and most closing stores were reopened or reused rather than left empty.

bench.title: SIMULATION: Let workers and towns buy a fresh start
bench.answer: If Poundland is sold in pieces, which could happen [s1], government should fund a local rescue scheme. Workers and local shoppers would jointly own rescued shops, with one vote each. Councils would offer capped loans only where a plan shows sales can cover wages, rent and repayments. Money would buy shop assets, never shares in the failing owner. The same scheme would advance unpaid wages within two weeks and fund training where shops cannot survive. Each town would publish costs, repayments and jobs kept after a year. Success means workers paid promptly and shops covering their bills without repeat support.

gate.verdict: No answer passes every test: A and B each pass the pay limits, and none of the three clearly settles both retraining and reuse of empty shops. What facts cannot settle is who should carry the risk of keeping stores open.

jury.question: When a big chain fails, who should carry the risk of keeping its stores open: the state, the workers and towns, or nobody?
options: Workers are paid first and the stores go
Staff and councils get first call on closing stores
Worker and shopper co-owned shops, with public loans
Leave it to buyers; the state only pays what is owed
jury.ruling: Staff and councils get first call on closing stores (4 of 12). The jurors liked a cheap try that keeps shops from sitting empty without paying the owner.

reasons.text: Give staff and the council first go at a shop. Cheap to try, and I'd rather see it reopen than sit empty.
A short first right for staff and councils keeps shops open without paying the owners. That is sensible.
I need the workers paid quickly. Shops cannot be my first worry when wages are owed.
I ran things for years. Pay the workers their due, then let the market sort the shops. Councils run shops badly.

minister.trial: In one council area that loses a big-chain store in administration, staff and the council get 28 days of first call on the empty unit, and the Insolvency Service's 6-week pay aim is tracked for every eligible employee. Contractors' pay is only logged, not changed.
minister.fail_number: Fails if fewer than 1 in 4 closing stores get a staff or council bid in 28 days, or any eligible claim takes over 6 weeks.
minister.statement: Four of twelve jurors said staff and the council should get first call on a closing shop. Not the biggest win, so we start small. One council area. 28 days. No money to the owner or the bosses. The wages the law already promises get paid in 6 weeks, and we count every one. The people who stack the shelves know the shop better than any rival. Ask the board why they never asked.
